vignette:
Nabil is a 55-year-old married Middle Eastern American man who has spent most of his adult life farming. He lives with his wife on land that has structured his days for years: early mornings, animals to tend, equipment to check, long hours outdoors where work usually feels straightforward and physical. The assault happened there, on ground that had always felt familiar. He describes it only in broken stretches. What emerges is that he encountered another man on or near the farm, and that at some point Nabil registered the other man as behaving in a way that felt wrong-watchful, guarded, suspicious. He remembers his own body reacting first: his heart pounding hard enough to fill his awareness. He remembers the close smell of sweat, sharp and human, and then the sense of being overpowered. After that, the memory breaks apart. He can give flashes, not a full account. When he tries to tell it in sequence, he loses the thread and stops, frustrated and embarrassed, as if the story refuses to stay in his hands.

In the weeks after the assault, what disturbed him was not only what had happened but how strangely it sat in his mind. He would have isolated images or bodily impressions with nothing to connect them. At times the memory felt oddly detached, as if it were something he had heard about happening to another man rather than lived through himself. He knew, rationally, that it was his experience, yet when the fragments came back they carried an unreal quality that unsettled him. His wife would ask what exactly happened, and he would begin with confidence, then falter, circle back, and finally wave a hand in irritation because he could not make it coherent enough to say aloud.

Daily life on the farm put him in repeated contact with things that now jolted him. During heavy work, when he was lifting feed, repairing fencing, or moving quickly in the heat, his own heart racing could suddenly feel alarming rather than ordinary. In those moments he became acutely aware of the pounding in his chest and was pulled toward the assault before he had time to think. Sweat had changed meaning too. The smell of his own work clothes after a long morning, or the odor coming off another laborer nearby, could turn his stomach and bring back those disconnected pieces of the attack. He found himself scanning people more closely than before. If a man lingered near the property line, avoided eye contact, or moved in a way Nabil read as furtive, Nabil's attention locked on him immediately. He was certain he had to stay alert around people who seemed suspicious, even in ordinary interactions.

He did not talk much about the assault, but in his mind he returned to it relentlessly. A large part of that thinking took the form of revenge. He would replay what he knew and did not know, imagining how he might identify the assailant, confront him, make him pay, settle something that remained intolerably open. These thoughts occupied him while driving the tractor, checking irrigation, or lying awake after a long day. Alongside that, he began organizing his calendar around not noticing certain dates. As the anniversary of the assault approached, and other dates linked in his mind to what happened, he kept himself busy and tried to move through them as if they were ordinary. He did not want his wife mentioning them. He did not want to mark them, reflect on them, or leave room in the day for memory.

Work became his main way of getting through. He threw himself into farm tasks with a force his family noticed. If there was a fence to mend, he mended three. If machinery needed maintenance, he extended the job. He stayed outside longer, took on extra physical labor, and filled quiet periods before they could open into thought. This had costs. His wife saw less of him even though they lived and worked on the same property. Meals grew shorter. He was more absent in conversation, either preoccupied or too tired to engage. The farm benefited from his relentless pace, but the household felt tighter and more distant around him.

By the time he sought help, Nabil had grown worn down by the combination of bodily jolts, broken memory, and the sense that his mind kept circling something unfinished. What finally brought him in was not a single new incident so much as the recognition that he could no longer tell the story of what happened without unraveling, and that even on his own land he was living in anticipation of the next moment his chest would pound or someone would seem suspicious. He wants, above all, to be able to speak about the assault without losing himself halfway through. What frightens him most is that the memory will remain in pieces forever, and that he will go on organizing his life around work, watchfulness, and dates he cannot bear to face.
